obtained.how: the lake association's own free PDFs (belgradelakesassociation.org), all four reports; the 2020, 2023 and 2024 texts are indexed as <key>.y2020 / .y2023 / .y2024

bibliography.checked_against: the cover and title page of each report
bibliography.corrections: All four reports (not only 2024) were prepared by Lee Attix, Loon Conservation Associates, and submitted to the Belgrade Lakes Association: 2019 report submitted 5 December 2019; 2020 report 2 December 2020; 2023 report 30 December 2023; 2024 report 2 January 2025. Each cover reads '<year> Belgrade Lakes Common Loon Monitoring Summary Report'. Suggested form: Attix, L. (Loon Conservation Associates) 2019, 2020, 2023, 2025. <Year> Belgrade Lakes Common Loon Monitoring Summary Report. Report to the Belgrade Lakes Association. The in-text citation '(Belgrade Lakes Association 2019–2024)' (§3.8.2) implies a run of years; only 2019, 2020, 2023 and 2024 are cited.
bibliography.note: show.mjs found no in-text match because the paper writes '(Belgrade Lakes Association 2019–2024)', split across lines 1056–1057 of 03_synthesis_fish_to_forest.md (§3.8.2).

claims.claim: At the Belgrade Lakes in 2019, 23 territorial pairs on two lakes fledged 0.35 young per pair
claims.location: 2019 report, PDF p. 3 (report p. 2), Executive summary; PDF p. 7 (report p. 6), section 6.1 and Table 1
claims.quote: Overall productivity was 0.35 fledged young per territorial pair
claims.conditions: Great Pond and Long Pond, Kennebec County; surveys May–August by boat or shore, six professional visits plus volunteer surveys; 'fledged' = chick surviving > 6 weeks; 23 territorial pairs, 14 nested, 9 successful nests, 8 chicks fledged

claims.claim: the two lakes are about 1,000 and 3,300 ha
claims.note: None of the four reports gives lake areas. The areas come from elsewhere: the research note (shore_birds_and_mammals.md) gives Long Pond 2,557 acres (LakesOfMaine; ≈ 1,035 ha) and Great Pond 8,239 acres (IF&W survey map; ≈ 3,334 ha). Cite those for the areas.

claims.claim: natural nests succeeded in up to 54 % of attempts (upper end of 22–54 %, four years 2019–2024)
claims.location: 2019 report, PDF p. 3 (report p. 2), Executive summary
claims.quote: only seven of 13 natural nests (54%) were successful
claims.conditions: both lakes, 2019; rafts excluded (2 of 2 raft nests succeeded)
claims.note: The same report's section 6.2 (PDF p. 12) gives 4 of 7 natural nests (57 %) for Long Pond alone; the 54 % is the two-lake figure.

claims.claim: natural nests succeeded in as few as 22 % of attempts (lower end of 22–54 %)
claims.location: 2020 report, PDF p. 3 (Executive summary); 2023 report, PDF p. 3; 2024 report, PDF p. 3
claims.quote: nine natural nest attempts on the two lakes and only two nests were successful
claims.conditions: both lakes; 2020: 2/9 (22 %); 2023: 9/18 (50 %); 2024: 6/15 (40 %); raft nests counted separately
claims.note: Range over the four reported years 22–54 % holds. Productivity in the later years: 0.17 (2020), 0.26 (2023), 0.26 (2024) fledged young per territorial pair, with 23 territorial pairs every year.

claims.claim: that spacing, one pair per 94–278 ha, implies roughly 1–4 pairs on Upper's 360–370 ha (project arithmetic)
claims.quote: Twelve territorial pairs were identified on Great Pond
claims.conditions: 2019 counts: Great Pond 12 territorial pairs, Long Pond 11
claims.note: Long Pond ≈ 1,035 ha / 11 pairs = 94 ha per pair; Great Pond ≈ 3,334 ha / 12 = 278 ha per pair; 365 ha / 278 = 1.3 and 365 / 94 = 3.9, so 1–4 pairs. Pair counts checked here; the lake areas are not from these reports (see the area claim). In later years the split was Great 13 / Long 10 (2023, 2024), giving 256 and 104 ha per pair — the 1–4 conclusion is unchanged.

notes: PRIVACY: the reports name each loon territory and nest site (islands, coves); none is written here. Internal inconsistencies in the 2019 report: chicks hatched 13 (executive summary) vs 15 (section 6.1 and Table 1); nesting pairs 14 (summary, results) vs 15 (discussion); the paper's figures (0.35, 54 %) are unaffected. In the 2023 report the executive summary says 9 successful nests, the results 10 (9 natural + 1 raft). Recorded failure causes in 2019: two mammalian predation, four unknown; no flooding losses in 2019. The 2019 discussion calls 0.35 'well below the established sustainable population threshold of 0.48 CH/TP' — a figure the paper could use.
